title: PathCRF: Ball-Free Soccer Event Detection via Possession Path Inference from Player Trajectories

problem.claim: Soccer event data collection relies heavily on labor-intensive manual annotation.

gap.claim: Ball tracking is difficult to scale because of high infrastructural and operational costs, confining comprehensive data collection largely to top-tier competitions.

contributions.claim: PathCRF detects on-ball soccer events using only player tracking data.
The framework models player trajectories as a fully connected dynamic graph and selects exactly one edge representing the current possession state at each time step.
A Conditional Random Field constrains edge transitions, with dynamically computed emission and transition scores, and Viterbi decoding produces the most probable edge sequence.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that PathCRF produces accurate and logically consistent possession paths.
The authors report that the resulting possession paths enable downstream analyses while substantially reducing the need for manual event annotation.
The authors state that source code is available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Manual annotation remains labor-intensive, while ball tracking is costly to scale.
These constraints limit comprehensive soccer data collection to top-tier competitions.
PathCRF infers possession paths from player trajectories using a dynamic graph and CRF-constrained edge selection.
Viterbi decoding yields an edge sequence, with event detections triggered by changes between adjacent selected edges.
The authors report accurate, logically consistent paths and reduced annotation needs.

source_observation.claim: The framework detects events from player tracking data without requiring ball tracking.

interpretation.claim: When a costly sensing modality limits scale, structured inference from more available trajectories may provide a scalable alternative.

application.claim: Apply constrained sequence inference to derive interaction events from agent trajectories in settings where direct object tracking is expensive.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish performance across competitions, tracking qualities, or event types beyond the reported setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, sample sizes, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the socio-temporal backbone architecture in detail.
The abstract does not establish generalization beyond soccer or the reported experimental setting.
